It reads as an institutional/technical policy report rather than a peer‑reviewed journal article, conference paper or preprint.
title: Quantum computing and the financial system: opportunities and risks
journal_or_venue: Bank for International Settlements (BIS) Papers No 149, Monetary and Economic Department
abstract_summary: This BIS technical paper reviews how quantum computing could transform finance by enabling faster solutions for complex problems—such as risk simulation, portfolio optimisation, macroeconomic modelling and enhanced AI—while also posing significant cyber risks. A major concern is quantum-capable attacks on widely used public-key cryptography and 'harvest now, decrypt later' threats, prompting recommendations for early adoption of quantum-resistant cryptography and initiatives like Project Leap to prepare the financial sector.
methodology_description: This paper is a narrative/technical review and policy-oriented synthesis rather than an empirical or experimental study. The authors conducted a literature survey of academic papers, working papers, technical reports and industry sources on quantum computing and its implications for finance and cryptography. They compiled and synthesised evidence from peer-reviewed research (eg, journal articles and arXiv preprints), central bank and BIS work (including a BIS central-bank survey), industry press releases and roadmaps (eg, IBM, Atom Computing, NEC), patent databases (PATENTSCOPE), market research reports, Google Trends and Google Scholar query counts, and existing expert/professional surveys (eg, Mosca & Piani 2023). The paper also draws on results and early findings from BIS Project Leap and other referenced experimental studies (summarised from the literature). Quantitative elements are limited to descriptive trend graphs constructed from publicly available sources and simple illustrative calculations (eg, an aggregate market projection for high-performance computing, a back-of-the-envelope estimate of potential cost savings under assumed percent improvements, and an expected-loss calculation obtained by multiplying central-bank survey estimates of maximum potential loss by expert-probability estimates of cryptographic breakage). No original quantum algorithms were developed or run by the authors. The authors used qualitative synthesis to identify application areas, risks and policy implications, and they acknowledge limitations and uncertainty in timelines and scale. (The authors also note the use of GPT-4 only for proofreading and style edits.)
key_findings: [supported] Experimental quantum devices reached ~1,000 physical qubits in 2023–24 (Atom Computing, IBM announcements).
[speculative] Roadmaps from vendors (eg, IBM) project 2,000 logical qubits and aim to deliver full-scale quantum capability beyond 2033.
[supported] Qubits exploit superposition and entanglement and can be described as representing 2^n basis states in superposition (basic quantum-mechanical fact).

[speculative] Quantum computers will provide large computational speedups for a narrow subset of problems (eg, simulation, optimisation, search) while complementing classical computers for general tasks.
[supported] Public attention, VC investment and patent activity in quantum computing have grown strongly in recent years (documented by Google Trends, PitchBook, patents).
[supported] There is no consensus that a practically useful, large-scale quantum computer has already been achieved; claims (eg, Google 2019) are contested in the literature.
[supported] Expert surveys (Mosca & Piani 2023) estimate a cryptographically relevant quantum computer could appear within roughly 5–30 years (probabilities provided in survey).
[supported] Families of quantum algorithms (eg, quantum Fourier transform, amplitude amplification, quantum walks) are established in the literature.

[speculative] Quantum algorithms can offer quadratic or greater speedups for financial tasks such as Monte Carlo simulations, derivative pricing and risk metrics (paper reports potential quadratic speedups in some cases).
[speculative] Quantum computing may enable new financial use cases currently infeasible with classical computing (eg, high-dimensional systemic risk analysis, new macroeconomic solution methods).

[supported] Several small-scale empirical demonstrations show quantum or hybrid devices can outperform classical methods on specific benchmark problems (examples cited include quantum-annealer results and experimental reinforcement-learning tasks).

[speculative] Integrating quantum computing with AI (quantum ML, quantum reinforcement learning, quantum deep learning) could materially enhance machine-learning performance, but practical benefits remain uncertain.

[supported] Data loading (initialisation) into quantum states and extracting information from quantum outputs (measurement) are known bottlenecks limiting practical advantage for many real-world problems.

[speculative] Short-term economic benefits of quantum computing are likely modest and concentrated in a small set of use cases; long-term transformational impacts are possible but uncertain (analogy to electrification/internet).
[supported] Shor's algorithm theoretically breaks widely used asymmetric cryptography (RSA, ECC) given a sufficiently large, error-corrected quantum computer.
[supported] Grover's algorithm gives only limited speedup against symmetric-key schemes, so increasing symmetric key lengths can mitigate quantum threats to symmetric encryption.
[supported] The 'harvest now, decrypt later' (HNDL) threat is a present concern: adversaries can store intercepted encrypted data today to decrypt in the future once quantum capability exists.
[supported] NIST-led post-quantum cryptography standardisation is underway; first algorithm selections were announced (2022) and initial standards published (August 2024).

[supported] Quantum key distribution (QKD) and other quantum-physics-based cryptographic techniques offer complementary opportunities to strengthen security but face practical scalability, distance and cost limitations today.

[supported] Migrating complex legacy financial and central bank IT systems to quantum-resistant cryptography is technically complex, resource-intensive and time-consuming; planning and early action are necessary.

[supported] Project Leap (BIS Innovation Hub, Banque de France, Deutsche Bundesbank) demonstrated successful VPN connections using post-quantum cryptography but observed measurable additional latency during key-setup operations.

[supported] Empirical/experimental studies report sizable but context-specific speedups: e.g., Fernández-Villaverde & Hull (2023) solved an RBC model on a quantum annealer in ~3% of the time of a classical implementation.

[speculative] Many published quantum-finance algorithms and performance estimates are theoretical or based on emulation/hybrid devices; practical quantum advantage for real-world, large-scale financial tasks remains to be demonstrated.

[supported] Survey-based central-bank estimates and expert-probability inputs imply expected GDP losses from a systemically relevant quantum-enabled cyber attack of roughly 0.1% of GDP within 5 years and potentially >1% within 15–20 years (depending on probability assumptions).
results_summary: The BIS technical report surveys the current state of quantum computing R&D and its potential benefits and risks for the financial system. It documents strong recent experimental progress (devices of ~1,000 qubits) and increased public/private activity, describes established quantum algorithms and proposed financial applications (risk, portfolio optimisation, payments, macro modelling, quantum-augmented AI), and highlights algorithmic and systems bottlenecks (data loading and measurement). The paper emphasises a credible, theoretically grounded cyber risk to existing public-key cryptography (Shor's algorithm) and documents ongoing mitigation efforts (NIST post-quantum standards, Project Leap tests). Overall, short-term, broadly applicable economic gains are judged modest and concentrated; however, long-run transformational potential exists alongside urgent needs to migrate to quantum-resistant cryptography because of the harvest-now–decrypt-later threat.

performance_claims.claim: Egger et al estimate a quantum computer could perform VaR calculations for a 1 million-asset portfolio in ~30 minutes (versus several hours classically).
McMahon et al (Bank of Canada) experimental hybrid quantum-annealing approach on a 30-day payments sample estimated liquidity savings of CAD 239.93 million to CAD 275.70 million.

Fernández-Villaverde & Hull (2023) report solving an RBC dynamic programming model on a quantum annealer in ~3% of the computation time of a traditional computer (an order-of-magnitude speedup in that experiment).
Back-of-envelope projection: global high-performance-computing market ~USD 90 billion in 10 years; a nominal 10% cost reduction from QC would imply USD 0.9 billion/year savings (illustrative).

Project Leap experiments implementing post-quantum algorithms in a VPN showed measurable additional latency (longer VPN key-setup times) compared with legacy cryptography (performance penalty varies by algorithm).

Survey-informed estimate: expected losses from a systemically relevant quantum-enabled cyber attack ~0.1% of GDP on average within five years; with increasing breach probability expected losses could exceed 1% of GDP within 15–20 years (survey-derived).

quantum_advantage_detail: The report presents theoretical and small-scale empirical demonstrations of quantum speedups for narrowly defined problems (eg, annealer results, small benchmark tasks) but concludes that broad, practical quantum advantage for real-world, large-scale financial problems has not yet been demonstrated and is likely to be limited to a small set of problems in the near term; long-run transformative potential remains uncertain.
limitations: Quantum computers are still in an experimental phase; practical, large-scale QCs are not yet available.
Maintaining qubit coherence is difficult: noise, decoherence and error rates require many physical qubits per logical qubit, raising resource demands.
Uncertainty about timing: expert estimates for cryptographically relevant QCs vary widely (eg 5–30 years).
Quantum computing is suited only to a narrow subset of computational tasks; it will not replace classical computing for general-purpose workloads.
Many proposed quantum algorithms remain theoretical or have only been tested on emulators/small prototypes; demonstrated, real-world quantum speedups are limited.
Data initialisation (encoding classical data into quantum states) and output measurement (extracting useful classical information) are significant bottlenecks that can offset algorithmic speedups.
Short-term economic benefits are modest and concentrated: most practical gains are limited to very large or specialised problems.
Scalability, integration and cost challenges for quantum cryptography (eg QKD): long-distance transmission, network infrastructure and high implementation costs impede near-term deployment.
Migration to post-quantum cryptography is complex, time-consuming and resource-intensive; legacy systems may be incompatible and require extensive adaptation.

Post-quantum cryptography can introduce latency and performance penalties (empirical tests such as Project Leap show increased setup/handshake times), which may be problematic for low-latency financial services.
Quantifying economic impacts and losses from a quantum-enabled cyber event is uncertain; available estimates rely on expert surveys and contain wide uncertainty.
The ‘harvest now, decrypt later’ threat means sensitive data captured today may be vulnerable in the future, creating urgency despite the current immaturity of QCs.

#idea:near-term-feasibility — Short-term (NISQ-era) economic benefits are expected to be modest and concentrated in a few niche use cases; long-term transformational impacts are plausible but highly uncertain.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Empirical demonstrations and vendor roadmaps point to hybrid quantum-classical deployments and hybrid devices as the practical near-term path (eg, quantum annealers and hybrid experimental RL/optimisation results).

#idea:quantum-advantage — Small-scale empirical demonstrations have shown context-specific speedups (examples cited include annealer results and an RBC-model run reported to be ~3% of classical time), but these are not general-purpose proof-of-advantage.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Data-loading and measurement/extraction are highlighted as concrete bottlenecks that limit end-to-end quantum advantage for real-world financial datasets.

#idea:quantum-advantage — Shor's algorithm presents a clear and supported long-term threat to public-key cryptography; short-to-medium term mitigation (post-quantum crypto) is urgent because of 'harvest now, decrypt later'.

#idea:hybrid-approach — Project Leap and other initiatives demonstrate practical steps (eg, post-quantum VPNs) and measurable operational impacts (additional latency during key setup), underscoring deployment/transition costs.

contradictions: The report highlights small empirical demonstrations of quantum speedups (eg, an annealer solving an RBC model much faster) while also emphasising that many claimed advantages are contested and not generalisable — a tension between anecdotal experimental successes and the absence of consensus on practical superiority (see 2023_FernandezVillaverde_Hull_RBC and discussion of contested Google 2019 claims).

Vendor roadmaps projecting large-scale, error-corrected devices (eg, IBM 2,000 logical qubits beyond 2033) are presented alongside supported statements about severe scalability, error-correction and data-loading bottlenecks — the paper both reports optimistic timelines and stresses technical barriers that make those timelines uncertain.

The paper documents algorithmic speedup claims (eg, quadratic gains for Monte Carlo via amplitude amplification) but also notes that costly state preparation and readout can erase end-to-end advantages for realistic financial problems, contradicting simplistic interpretations of asymptotic speedups.
